name: CNAME cloaking
plain: A tracker is served from a subdomain of the site (like metrics.site.com) that points at the tracker's servers.
meaning: Makes tracking look first party so the cookie lasts longer and blockers miss it. Safari caps cookies set by such CNAME or mismatched IP hosts to 7 days. Studies found it on a few percent of top sites (Dimova et al 2021).

web.api: DNS CNAME to a third party plus Set-Cookie from that subdomain

access.persistence: Safari: 7 days. Others: cookie lifetime set by the tracker (up to 400 days in Chrome)
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

firefox.note: Blocked only with extensions that read CNAME

limits.headline: Can hide a tracker as part of the site's own address so it looks first party
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a page loads a script from a tracker disguised as the site
can: Serve a tracker from a name like metrics.site.com that points to a tracker's servers
Set cookies that look like the site's own
Last longer than third party cookies in some browsers
cannot: Stay hidden from Firefox and Safari, which check where the name really points
Work for browsers that block known tracker names
Get past a content blocker that checks the real destination
Follow you to other sites with the same cookie
limits.reach_label: A tracker disguised as the site
limits.differs: Firefox, Safari and some content blockers check where the name really points and limit it. Chrome mostly does not.

story.what_it_is: A tracker is made to look like part of the site you are visiting, using a disguised web address.

marketing.name: Tracking prevention
marketing.pitch: WebKit explains that Safari limits cookies set by hosts that use CNAME or other cloaking to hide third party trackers.

story.for_you: You never see it. The tracker's code loads from something like metrics.shop.com, which looks like the shop itself. Your blocker may not catch it, and its cookie may last longer.
story.for_makers: A site that wants longer cookies and fewer blocked requests points a subdomain at a tracker's servers. It looks first party. Browsers now limit such cookies to about a week, and blockers started to check the real address.

use_cases.example: A shop hosts its Adobe or Criteo tracker at a subdomain so blockers do not stop it.
A publisher's analytics vendor serves data collection from the publisher's own domain to keep cookies for longer.
An online store sets a tracker CNAME to follow shoppers from ad to checkout, even with blockers on.
A news site sets up a tag server on its domain, so its ad partners can set cookies as though they were the site.
A game portal hides its ad partner behind a subdomain so ads and player tracking are not blocked.
A privacy researcher uses DNS lookups to spot a hidden tracker behind a friendly sounding subdomain.

technical_bounds: Safari ITP limits CNAME or IP mismatched server cookies to 7 days
Browsers with DNS access (Firefox with uBlock Origin) can uncloak
Server must be delegated by the site

history.change: ITP caps cookies set via CNAME cloaked requests to 7 days
Dimova et al: CNAME tracking found on about 10% of 10,000 sites in a measurement (see paper)
